conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Maya—I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. Thank you for taking a few minutes with me today.

I’d like to use a quick questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or “EPDS” for short. It’s simply 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally during the past seven days. There’s no pass-or-fail; your honest answers let us know what kind of support might be helpful right now.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team. If any question feels uncomfortable, just let me know and we can slow down or skip it.

We’ll go through one question at a time. When you’re ready, here’s the first one:

**Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?**

I’ve been able to laugh, mostly. I mean, when my husband makes one of his goofy jokes or the baby does something funny—like that little milk-drunk face—I still chuckle. It’s not quite as easy or spontaneous as before, but it definitely hasn’t felt impossible.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
As much as I always could
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most of the time I still do—like when my mom said she’d come over for coffee this week I was excited, and I’m looking forward to taking the baby for his two-month pictures. It’s not every single moment, but I can still find things to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. Sometimes I’ll think, “Maybe I should’ve burped him longer,” if he spits up, but I don’t dwell on it. I know babies are unpredictable, so I shrug it off pretty quickly.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit. Like last night I suddenly worried that his breathing sounded different, even though he was fine. It only lasted a few minutes and then I was able to tell myself it’s normal newborn stuff, but yes—those random worries do pop up now and then.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt jittery once or twice when the baby startled and cried loudly—my heart races, but it settles right away. I haven’t had any real panic feelings.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. Like when he skips a nap and I’m trying to wash bottles one-handed while he’s fussing, it feels a bit overwhelming, but it passes once I sit down and give him the pacifier. Overall I still manage to get through the day’s to-do list.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been one of the better parts. Once he settles for the night—usually after the 2 a.m. feed—I drift right back off. I haven’t felt so unhappy that it kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
Hardly at all. I might feel a bit blue for a minute if I’m really tired, but it lifts quickly—especially when the baby gives me one of those little sleepy smiles.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, not really. I teared up a little on day five when my milk came in and my breasts felt like rocks, but that was more about pain than sadness, and it passed once I got a warm compress on them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to be here for my baby and watch him grow—that thought hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Screening Note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) Interview
Date: [today]

Symptom profile:
- Mood: denies persistent sadness, crying spells, sleep-disruption due to low mood, or anhedonia; reports brief “blue” minutes when fatigued
- Anxiety: mild, situation-specific worries (e.g., infant breathing) without panic attacks; physical startle response resolves quickly
- Guilt/self-blame: minimal and transient; attributes infant issues to normal variability
- Coping: occasional overwhelmed feelings when routine disrupted; able to self-soothe and complete daily tasks
- Sleep: no difficulty falling back to sleep after infant feeds
- Safety: denies self-harm ideation; protective toward infant

Patterns:
Overall preserved capacity for pleasure, laughter, and future-oriented thinking; situational rather than pervasive distress; no neuro-vegetative signs of depression.

Screening significance:
Current responses do not suggest clinically significant postpartum depression or anxiety; no safety concerns identified at this time. Continue routine postpartum support and re-screen if clinical picture changes.
